title: The Way We Sleep
blurb: Talk about past and present habits

steps.html:
Thirteen hours in the air, earplugs in, and not a wink. Then a woman who has spent years in a town where the sun does not rise for two months, explaining what that actually does to a daily routine.

  • Follow two personal accounts of sleep and routine
  • Use used to, would and the present simple for habits
  • Use the idioms English has for sleeping and not sleeping
  • Write about how your own habits have changed

steps.title: used to, would, and the present simple
steps.html:
Three ways of saying 'this is what happens' or 'this is what used to happen'.

For a present habit, use the present simple, usually with a frequency adverb: I always get up at six. I never nod off on trains. The present continuous with always means something different — it complains: He's always falling asleep in meetings.

For a past habit that has stopped, use used to + infinitive: I used to sleep like a log. It works for both actions and states.

Would + infinitive also describes a repeated past action, and is common in narrative: Every winter we would put the lights on at two in the afternoon. But would does not work for past states: I would be a light sleeper is wrong. Only used to covers be, have, know, live, like.

Do not confuse three similar forms. used to do = a past habit. be used to doing = accustomed to it now. get used to doing = becoming accustomed. I used to live in Tromsø. I am used to living in the dark. I got used to it after two winters.

The negative and question forms of used to drop the d: I didn't use to sleep well. Did you use to nod off?

Question — again no d.

A past state — only used to, never would be.

I got used to living without a sunrise.
-ing after get used to.

He's always nodding off in meetings.
Continuous + always: a complaint.

steps.title: Choosing between used to, would and be used to
steps.html:
1. The facts: before you had children you slept nine hours; you no longer do; you have now adapted to five.
  2. 'Slept nine hours' is a past habit that has stopped: I used to sleep nine hours.
  3. You could also say I would sleep nine hours — a repeated action, so would is allowed here.
  4. But 'I was a heavy sleeper' is a state, so only one form works: I used to be a heavy sleeper. Never I would be.
  5. 'I have now adapted' is a present state: I am used to five hours now. Note the -ing if a verb follows: I am used to sleeping five hours.

steps.title: You are going to write about a habit that has changed.
Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Describe the old habit, the change, and the situation now. Use used to, would, be used to and the present simple at least once each.
steps.placeholder: Until I was about … I used to …
steps.html:
• Describe the old habit with <i>used to</i>.
  • Add a repeated past action with <i>would</i>.
  • Describe the change and how long it took, with <i>get used to</i>.
  • Describe the situation now, with the present simple and <i>be used to</i>.

Useful language

  • I used to … , and I never used to …
  • Every winter / every Sunday we would …
  • It took me about … to get used to …
  • I'm used to it now, though I still …
  • These days I usually … , and I hardly ever …
  • I'm always …-ing, which drives my family mad.
steps.modelHtml:
Six o'clock

Until I was about twenty-six I used to sleep like a log for nine hours and get up at ten with no memory of the night at all. At university my flatmates would knock on the door at midday to check I was alive.

Then I started a job that began at seven, and for about four months it was miserable. I didn't use to mind alarms; suddenly I hated them. I would lie awake from four, worrying about not sleeping, which of course is the one thing that guarantees you will not.

It took roughly a year to get used to it. Now I get up at six without an alarm, I'm used to being awake before anybody else in the building, and on the rare Sunday when I have a lie-in I feel worse, not better.
